searchText: <@273808422753796097> Can you give a bit more clarity on what "within reach" means here? **vbuterin** As in, an attacker willing to burn millions of dollars can generate a collision **vbuterin** And of course that cost will keep decreasing over time Hmm, it only costs millions (as in, single digit millions) to generate one collision? Not targeted collisions though, right? This is just "I found two private keys that result in a single address"? You wouldn't, however, be able to find a collision for address X with only millions of dollars? The more addresses in use, the more likely a collision becomes too **jadler** You still have 160 bits of preimage resistance with 20-byte addresses. The 80 bits of security is only for collisions. Even with 1 trillion accounts you'd have effectively 160-12=148 bits of preimage resistance. So "more addresses in use" doesn't really mean much (that's kind of the point of so many bits of security). **vbuterin** The collision resistance really matters **vbuterin** It's critical for usecases that involve not-yet-published contracts **jadler** (in reply to **vbuterin**) Hmmm could you expand on the specific attack vector you have in mind? **vbuterin** Give someone an address, claiming it represents one contract, but then actually publish a different code that maps to the same address **vbuterin** This is assuming create2 based conrtact creation **vbuterin** State channels rely on unique address -> code mapping heavily **jadler** (in reply to **vbuterin**) Makes sense Maybe don't accept contracts that have a nonce that can obviously be farmed? 😬 I *think* (correct me if wrong) in order to farm in "reasonable" time (even for a powerful actor) you have to be able to mutate both. You can't reasonably farm one until it matches an expected. So if someone gives you a yet-to-be-deployed contract that has some constant that could be anything... perhaps you shouldn't accept it. Though, 🤔, I suppose such contracts likely have some recipient address in them, and that recipient address can be farmed. OK, I'm convinced that farming such contracts is reasonable and non-obvious.
